one_liner: Go hash-and-displace minimal perfect hash for fixed string sets; author reports 25-50% faster index lookups than a Go map.
what_it_does: Takes a []string known up front and builds a static function that maps each key to its position in that slice (0..N-1). The whole API is mph.New(keys) *Table and (*Table).Query(key) int32, and values live in your own slice indexed by the result. It is not a map replacement: there is no insert or delete, no stored keys and no found flag, so a key outside the set gets back a valid-looking index unless you compare it against keys[idx] yourself. Table.Values and Table.Seeds are exported []int32 slices (since PR #6, 2020), so a built table can be written to disk or emitted as Go source by go generate.
how_it_is_fast: It is a simplified, uncompressed form of hash-and-displace from Belazzougui, Botelho and Dietzfelbinger's 'Hash, Displace, and Compress' (CHD), with one bucket per slot chosen by the low bits of a 64-bit MetroHash. For each multi-key bucket, largest first, New brute-forces a seed so that xorshift-multiply(hash+seed) sends every key in the bucket to a free slot, while single-key buckets skip the search and store their slot directly as a negative seed. A Query is one MetroHash of the key (avo-generated assembly on amd64 via go-metro, pure Go elsewhere), a bitmask into Seeds, an optional xorshift-multiply, and a load from Values: two array reads, no probing and no key comparison. The arrays are padded to a power of two so the slot comes from a mask instead of a modulo.
when_to_use: Static string sets fixed at build time or startup (protocol commands, keywords, dictionary words, ID or enum tables) where you need a key-to-dense-index mapping and keep payloads in a parallel slice.
Hot read paths where every queried key is guaranteed to be in the set. Skipping the key comparison is safe there, and it is part of where the speed comes from.
Sets from a few keys up to a few million held in RAM. Construction is linear, and the author reports 100-125 ms for about 235k words.

Tables you want to precompute and ship. The exported Values/Seeds slices can be serialized, mmapped (the author's suggestion) or generated as Go source, and go-metro reads input little-endian, so hashes match across architectures.
When you want about 140 lines of MIT-licensed code you can read in full and vendor, rather than a larger MPHF library.
when_not_to_use: Queries that may include unknown keys. Query returns an arbitrary in-range index for them, so you have to keep the keys and compare, which gives back part of the speedup. cespare/mph does that check inside Lookup.
Key sets that change at runtime. There is no insert or delete, so any change means a full rebuild that needs every key up front.

Tight memory budgets or very large sets. Values and Seeds together take 8 bytes per power-of-two slot, which is 8-16 bytes per key (about 2 MB for 235k words). PTHash, PtrHash and RecSplit need roughly 2-3 bits per key, and the author's own go-boomphf needs 3.7 bits per key.
Non-string keys. New accepts only []string, so integer or struct keys must be encoded to strings first.
Anything that needs a maintained dependency. The repo has no go.mod, no tags, 3 known importers on pkg.go.dev, and a 2025 bug-fix PR that nobody has reviewed.

integration.min_toolchain: Not documented. There is no go.mod, so it resolves to pseudo-version v0.0.0-20211217222804-81a8625fb7ed. The code uses sort.Slice (Go 1.8+). go-metro's amd64 stub file carries only a //go:build constraint, so Go 1.17+ is the safe floor.
integration.platforms: Any Go target. MetroHash runs as avo-generated assembly on amd64 with the gc compiler (unless the purego or noasm tag is set) and as pure Go elsewhere. No results are published for any platform.
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. New builds a fresh Table and Query only reads the Seeds and Values slices, so concurrent Queries on a finished Table look safe from the source.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — it replaces only a read-only map[string]int-style index in which every queried key is known to be present. Query returns an index rather than a value, has no ok result, and the table cannot be modified.

gotchas: Duplicate keys make New hang. Two identical keys always hash to the same slot, so the seed search for their bucket can never succeed, and it has no iteration cap or error return. Deduplicate first; the open PR #7 adds a duplicate check.
Query derives its mask from len(Values), so a hand-built or deserialized Table needs equal-length, power-of-two Values and Seeds. A zero-value Table panics with index out of range.
Open PR #7 (Aug 2025, unmerged, no reproducer) reports occasional out-of-bounds panics in Query's negative-seed (singleton) branch. The root cause is not documented.
A persisted table only works with the same hash: go-metro's MetroHash64 with seed 0. Swapping the hash, as PR #7 does with xxhash, invalidates saved tables.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick go-mph over cespare/mph, the other Go CHD-style entry, when you need to serialize or code-generate the table (cespare's fields are private) or every key is known to be present, since go-mph then does one full-key hash and no string compare per query where cespare does two Murmur3 hashes and a compare. Pick cespare/mph when absent keys are possible, and PTHash, PtrHash or RecSplit (about 2-3 bits/key) when memory or scale matters more than staying in pure Go.
verified_claims_summary: The only go-mph-versus-map evidence is prose in the author's December 2017 Gopher Academy post: about 25% faster than a Go map for 16 keys and 50% faster for the ~235k entries of /usr/dict/words, with no ns/op, Go version, CPU or flags given, against the pre-Swiss-table map that Go 1.24 replaced. The repo's BenchmarkMPH/BenchmarkMap pair compares an unverified index lookup with a map[string]int32 lookup that does compare keys, and the post's 20.4 vs 172 ns/op table measures a toy multiplier hash, not go-mph.
status_note: Abandoned: the last commit (2021-12-17) was a test-name tweak, the author's own 2018 serialization and space-optimization issues are still open, and an Aug 2025 fix PR is unreviewed, but it is a single 140-line MIT file (plus the MIT go-metro) that is easy to vendor and patch.
